7	## 0. THE CORE STORY IN ONE PARAGRAPH (the solution, established by r04/r06/r07 and confirmed by r10/r11/r14)
8	
9	The Ostrey Hollow skimming station's milk-test pipettes were short. They were blown for 17.6 c.c. but delivered a mean of 16.72 c.c. — 95 hundredths (one part in twenty short). Because a butterfat test bottle's neck is ruled to read percent for one specific charge and no other, every test made with that glass read 95% of the truth. The station's recorded average of 3.61 was really 3.80. The shortfall was **proportional, not fixed** — the station lost a twentieth of whatever was there, so it fell hardest on the richest milk. The missing fat was never stolen: it went down the valley in the cream and was entered in the Association's own ledgers, year by year, as "station gain." Nobody watered milk; nobody stole cream. The glass was condemned 12 June 1923 by state inspector Merle Strawn; tests rose immediately and permanently; Ansel Keddie was dismissed anyway in 1925; the cause was found by Ivy Keddie in 1958 and printed in Bulletin No. 471 (October 1958).
